text: Mobile gaming has become one of the fastest-growing forms of video content, driven by live streaming, recorded gameplay and cloud gaming services. Yet gaming video differs markedly from natural video: it is synthetically rendered, often contains sharp edges, overlaid text and rapid motion, and is viewed on small, high-resolution screens. Existing video quality assessment (VQA) models, which were developed largely for camera-captured content, may therefore fail to predict how players perceive distortions in this setting. To address this gap, we construct a new mobile gaming video database comprising source sequences from a diverse set of popular game genres, each processed with multiple codecs, resolutions and bitrates. A large-scale subjective study conducted on mobile devices yields mean opinion scores for every sequence. Benchmarking established full-reference and no-reference VQA algorithms against these scores reveals substantial limitations. We further propose an objective quality model tailored to gaming content that achieves state-of-the-art correlation with human judgments. The database will be made publicly available.

1. **Smash it on toast.** Spread mashed avocado on toasted sourdough and top it with flaky salt, chili flakes, a squeeze of lemon, and a fried or jammy egg if you want.

2. **Make guacamole.** Mash it with lime juice, diced onion, cilantro, jalapeño, and salt. Fold in chopped tomato just before serving.

3. **Blend it into a smoothie.** Half an avocado with banana, spinach, and milk or yogurt makes a thick, creamy smoothie that keeps you full longer.

4. **Turn it into a pasta sauce.** Blend avocado with garlic, basil, lemon juice, olive oil, and a splash of pasta water for a quick no-cook sauce.

5. **Bake it into chocolate mousse.** Blend avocado with cocoa powder, maple syrup or honey, vanilla, and a pinch of salt, then chill it. The avocado flavor disappears and you're left with a rich, silky dessert.

Social media is not inherently evil, but for teenagers its costs currently outweigh its benefits. I therefore agree that it does more harm than good.

The strongest argument concerns mental health. Platforms are engineered to maximize attention through endless feeds, notifications, and visible metrics like likes and follower counts. For adolescents, whose sense of identity is still forming, these features turn self-worth into a public scoreboard. Rising rates of anxiety and depression among teens, particularly girls, have tracked the spread of smartphones closely enough that many researchers now treat the link as more than coincidence.

Sleep and attention suffer as well. A phone in the bedroom invites late-night scrolling, and constant switching between apps makes it harder to develop the sustained focus that homework and serious reading require.

Defenders point to real benefits: staying close to friends, finding supportive communities for isolated or marginalized young people, and sharing creative work. These advantages are genuine. However, most of them could be achieved through less manipulative tools, such as group chats or moderated forums, without the comparison-driven design of mainstream platforms.

Ultimately, the problem lies less in teenagers' choices than in products built to exploit developing brains. Until those products change, the harm outweighs the good.

Holidays: At Home or Abroad?

Many people have different opinion about holidays. Some people like to stay at home and relax, but other people want to travel to another country. In my opinion, I prefer to travel abroad, and I will explain why.

First, when I travel abroad I can learn many new things. Every country have its own culture, food and history. For example, two years ago I went to Japan with my family. I was very surprise because the streets were so clean and people was very polite. I also eat real sushi and ramen, and it was much more delicious than in my country. This kind of experience I cannot get if I stay at home.

Second, travelling abroad helps me to practice English. In my country I only use English in the class. But when I travel, I need to speak English in the hotel, in the restaurant and in the airport. Sometimes I make mistakes, but people are usually kind and they understand me. After the trip, I feel more confident for speaking.

Of course, staying at home also has some good points. It is more cheap and you don't need to worry about the plane or the luggage. You can sleep a lot and spend time with your friends. Sometimes I also like this, especially when I am very tired after exams.

However, I think holidays is a special time and we should use it for do something different. Travelling abroad give me memories that I will remember for all my life. That is why I prefer to travel abroad instead of staying at home.

Data can be stored in diamond by exploiting atomic-scale defects in its crystal lattice, most notably nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers, in which a nitrogen atom sits beside a missing carbon atom. These defects can exist in different electrical charge states, and precisely tuned laser pulses can switch the defects within a tiny targeted region from one state to another. Because each charge state fluoresces differently under illumination, a low-power reading laser can determine whether a given site represents a 0 or a 1. Focusing the laser at different depths allows information to be written in multiple layers, enabling three-dimensional storage. Owing to diamond's exceptional stability, data kept in darkness can persist for very long periods.

# Kristin Chenoweth and Alan Cumming to Host 2015 Tony Awards

NEW YORK — Kristin Chenoweth and Alan Cumming, two of Broadway's most recognizable performers, will host the 69th annual Tony Awards. The awards will be presented on June 7 at Radio City Music Hall in a ceremony airing live at 8 p.m. on CBS.

The pairing brings together two Tony Award winners whose careers span stage, film and television. Ms. Chenoweth won a Tony in 1999 for her performance as Sally Brown in "You're a Good Man, Charlie Brown" and went on to originate the role of Glinda in the musical "Wicked." She is also a nominee this season, competing for best actress in a musical for her performance in the revival of "On the Twentieth Century."

Mr. Cumming won the Tony Award for best actor in a musical in 1998 for his portrayal of the Emcee in "Cabaret," a role he reprised in the show's most recent Broadway revival. Television audiences know him as the political operative Eli Gold on the CBS drama "The Good Wife."

They succeed Hugh Jackman, who hosted last year's ceremony.

Among the evening's most closely watched categories is best play, in which four productions of markedly different character, ranging from pointed contemporary drama to sweeping historical epic, will compete.

"The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time," Simon Stephens's adaptation of Mark Haddon's best-selling novel, follows a 15-year-old mathematical prodigy who sets out to investigate the death of a neighbor's dog. The production transferred to Broadway from London's National Theatre.

"Disgraced," by Ayad Akhtar, examines identity, faith and ambition through a Manhattan dinner party that turns explosive. The play received the 2013 Pulitzer Prize for Drama.

"Hand to God," a dark comedy by Robert Askins, centers on a shy teenager in a Texas church puppet ministry whose sock puppet appears to develop a sinister personality of its own.

"Wolf Hall Parts One & Two," the Royal Shakespeare Company's two-part production adapted by Mike Poulton from Hilary Mantel's novels "Wolf Hall" and "Bring Up the Bodies," charts Thomas Cromwell's rise to power in the court of Henry VIII.

The field pairs two acclaimed British imports with two new American works.

In the musical categories, "Fun Home" and "An American in Paris" led all productions with 12 nominations apiece, setting up a competitive race for best musical.

As in previous years, the telecast is expected to feature performances from nominated musicals, offering a national television audience a glimpse of productions that many viewers may never see in person. For producers, the broadcast also represents a significant marketing opportunity, as a strong showing at the Tonys can substantially boost ticket sales.

The Tony Awards, presented annually by the American Theatre Wing and The Broadway League, recognize excellence in productions that opened on Broadway during the preceding season. Winners are selected by more than 800 voters drawn from across the theater industry.

We investigate the tunneling dynamics of a bosonic Josephson junction, realized by a Bose–Einstein condensate confined in a double-well potential, in which interwell tunneling is assisted by a single-mode optical cavity field. Within a two-mode approximation, we derive an effective Hamiltonian in which the tunneling amplitude depends on the intracavity photon number, yielding a coupled nonlinear atom–light system. Using both mean-field and full quantum treatments, we analyze the evolution of the population imbalance and the relative phase between the wells. We show that the cavity field provides a tunable control parameter that can drive transitions between Josephson oscillations and macroscopic quantum self-trapping, and that cavity-induced nonlinearity leads to bistable behavior and modified collapse-and-revival dynamics. Furthermore, the transmitted cavity field offers a nondestructive probe of the atomic tunneling dynamics.

**Exchange Programmes: Worth the Journey**

Taking part in a school or university exchange programme is, in most cases, an excellent idea. The main benefit is personal growth. Living in another country pushes students outside their comfort zone. They have to manage money, make new friends and solve everyday problems without their families nearby, and that builds independence and confidence quickly.

Exchanges also improve language skills far faster than classroom lessons. When you have to order food, ask for directions or join a group project in another language, you learn because you need to. In addition, students come home with a wider view of the world and a better understanding of different cultures, which employers and universities value.

Exchanges do have drawbacks. They can be expensive, homesickness is real, and some credits may not transfer. Even so, scholarships and careful planning can solve most of these problems. For students who are willing to adapt, an exchange is an investment that pays off for life.

**Navy Sailors to Serve on Three Carriers in a Single Tour**

About 1,200 U.S. Navy sailors are set to take part in an unusual rotation that will have them serve aboard three different aircraft carriers, each named after an American president, during a single tour of duty.

The Navy calls the maneuver a "three-hull swap." It involves the USS George Washington, the USS Ronald Reagan and the USS Theodore Roosevelt, three Nimitz-class carriers that are trading home ports as part of a long-planned reshuffling of the fleet.

The George Washington, which has been based in Yokosuka, Japan, since 2008, is heading to Virginia for a scheduled midlife refueling and overhaul, a process that will keep it out of service for several years. The Ronald Reagan, currently based in San Diego, will replace it as the Navy's forward-deployed carrier in Japan, while the Theodore Roosevelt will shift its home port from Norfolk, Virginia, to San Diego.

For the sailors involved, the result is a voyage that spans much of the globe. The swap will take them from Japan, around South America to Virginia, and then back west to San Diego.

The long route around the southern tip of South America is necessary because Nimitz-class carriers are too wide to fit through the Panama Canal.

Coordinating the move is a significant logistical challenge. Personnel and equipment must be shifted among the three ships, and many sailors' families will need to relocate as the carriers change home ports.

For the crews, it is also a rare experience. Most sailors serve aboard a single ship during an assignment; serving on three carriers in one tour, and sailing through waters that U.S. carriers seldom visit, is something few in the Navy will ever do.

Model predictive control (MPC) offers a natural framework for handling constraints, but its effectiveness depends on an accurate dynamics model and on optimizers capable of coping with nonconvex, nonsmooth costs. This paper presents a safe learning-based MPC scheme that combines a learned dynamics model with gradient-free trajectory optimization using the cross-entropy method (CEM). System dynamics are represented by a probabilistic neural network ensemble that captures epistemic uncertainty. To ensure constraint satisfaction during learning, sampled control sequences are evaluated against a safe set constructed from uncertainty-aware reachability bounds, and unsafe samples are discarded before the CEM sampling distribution is updated. We establish conditions under which recursive feasibility is preserved. Simulations on a cart-pole system and an autonomous vehicle path-tracking task show that the method achieves performance comparable to gradient-based learning MPC while substantially reducing constraint violations.

They make money indirectly: the product is free, but something attached to it isn't.

For browsers, that something is usually search. Whenever you type into the address bar, the default search engine shows you ads, so search companies pay to be that default. Google pays Mozilla hundreds of millions of dollars a year for the spot in Firefox, which accounts for most of Mozilla's revenue. Chrome mainly serves to steer people toward Google's own search and ads, and Microsoft uses Edge to promote Bing and its other services.

Linux works differently. The code is free, but companies such as Red Hat and Canonical sell businesses support contracts, guaranteed security updates, certification and consulting. Meanwhile, giants like Intel, IBM and Google pay engineers to improve Linux because their servers, cloud platforms and Android phones all run on it.

Stress is something almost every student experiences. One major cause is academic pressure. Tests, homework, and the fear of getting bad grades can make students feel like they are never doing enough. Another cause is lack of sleep, since many students stay up late finishing assignments or scrolling on their phones. Social pressure also matters, because students often worry about fitting in and compare themselves to others on social media.

There are ways to reduce this stress. Students can plan their time better by using a planner and breaking big assignments into smaller parts. Getting enough sleep and exercising regularly can improve mood and focus. Schools can help by spreading out test dates and offering counseling services. Parents can support their children by focusing on effort instead of only grades.

Stress cannot be removed completely, but with good habits and support, students can manage it in a healthy way.

Tidal locking only means the Moon keeps the same face toward Earth. It doesn't mean that face is shielded from space.

Earth is a tiny shield. From the Moon it looks about two degrees wide, covering less than 0.01% of the sky. Meteoroids arrive from every direction, so both hemispheres get hit at nearly the same rate.

The near side also isn't aimed at one fixed point in space. As the Moon circles Earth, that face sweeps through every direction each month, so nothing stays permanently "behind" Earth.

The far side isn't dark, either. It gets just as much sunlight as the near side; we simply can't see it from here.

The far side does look more cratered, but that's because ancient lava flows on the near side buried many older craters, forming the smooth, dark maria.

Dr. Peter Albright delivered the news the way some men hand out parking tickets: briskly, and with the faint air of having done her a favor.

"Six months," he said. "Perhaps less. I'd get your affairs in order, Mrs. Kowalczyk."

Edna Kowalczyk was eighty-one. She had buried a husband, two dogs, and a forty-year fondness for menthol cigarettes. She looked down at Dr. Albright's loafers, which had tassels, and decided right then that she would not be giving him the satisfaction.

"I'll see you in six months," she said.

"I'd hope so," he replied, already reaching for the next chart.

She went home and made a list. It was not a list of affairs to put in order. It was titled THINGS ALBRIGHT WILL HAVE TO HEAR ABOUT, and the first item was *Walk to the mailbox without the cane.*

It took three weeks. Her hip complained the entire time, and she told her hip, out loud, that it could take its complaints to Dr. Albright.

The second item was the county fair, where she intended to enter her rhubarb pie for the first time since 1997. The third was learning to use the tablet her granddaughter had given her, because she had heard you could leave reviews of doctors on the internet.

At the six-month appointment, Dr. Albright frowned at her bloodwork for a very long time.

"Well," he said. "This is unusual."

"Second place," Edna said. "For the pie. The woman who won is married to one of the judges. I'm appealing."

He didn't know what to say to that, so he told her to come back in three months.

She came back in three months. And three after that. Her granddaughter, Talia, started driving her to the appointments because she wanted to watch. Edna would sit bolt upright on the crinkly paper, Dr. Albright would study her numbers as though they had personally insulted him, and Talia would bite the inside of her cheek to keep from laughing.

"What's your secret?" a nurse asked her once in the hallway.

"Pettiness," Edna said. "Wildly underrated."

It wasn't the whole truth. There was also the pie, which took first place the following year, after the judge's wife retired. There was the tablet, on which she discovered Talia had been posting photos of her with captions like *my grandma is undefeated*. There was the spring she planted tomatoes she had no business expecting to eat, and ate them anyway, warm from the vine, with a little salt.

But spite was what had gotten her out of the chair that first morning, and Edna believed in giving credit where it was due.

Four years after the six-month prognosis, Dr. Albright announced his retirement. Edna sent a card. Inside, in careful cursive, she wrote: *Congratulations. I'll be here when you get back.*

Talia asked whether that was a little mean.

"Sweetheart," Edna said, cutting her a slice of pie, "it's a lot mean. That's the whole point."

In cold-weather climates, winter activities generally fall into a few categories:

**Snow sports**
- Downhill skiing and snowboarding
- Cross-country skiing and snowshoeing
- Sledding and tobogganing
- Snowmobiling

**Ice-based activities**
- Ice skating on rinks or frozen ponds
- Ice hockey and curling
- Ice fishing, often from small shelters on frozen lakes

**Casual outdoor fun**
- Building snowmen and snow forts
- Snowball fights
- Winter hiking and wildlife spotting

**Cultural traditions**
- Winter festivals, such as Quebec City's Winter Carnival or the Harbin Ice and Snow Festival in China
- Sauna sessions followed by a cold plunge, especially popular in Finland and other Nordic countries

**Indoor pastimes**
- Gathering with friends and family over hot drinks and comfort food
- Reading, crafts, and board games
- Visiting museums, theaters, and indoor sports facilities

Several of these began as necessities rather than hobbies. Skis and snowshoes, for example, were originally practical tools for traveling and hunting over deep snow.

Contemporary dance is a concert dance style that emerged in the mid-20th century. It combines elements of modern dance, ballet, jazz, and sometimes non-Western and street styles. Rather than following one fixed technique, it emphasizes versatility, experimentation, and personal expression.

**Where it came from**

It grew out of modern dance pioneers such as Martha Graham, Doris Humphrey, and José Limón, who rejected the rigid rules of classical ballet. Merce Cunningham pushed things further in the 1940s and '50s by separating movement from music and story, treating dance as something that could exist on its own terms. Later choreographers, including Pina Bausch, Trisha Brown, William Forsythe, and Crystal Pite, kept expanding what dance could be.

**Key characteristics**

- **Floor work:** Dancers often roll, slide, and move through the floor instead of staying upright.
- **Use of gravity and weight:** Movements may involve falling, releasing, and recovering, and are often fluid and grounded rather than lifted and light like ballet.
- **Contrasts:** Choreography moves between stillness and speed, tension and release, control and abandon.
- **Breath and the torso:** Motion often starts from the spine or core, with contractions, spirals, and curves.
- **Improvisation:** Many pieces are built partly from dancers' improvised material.
- **Freedom from conventions:** Bare feet are common, music may be classical, electronic, pop, or absent altogether, and works don't need to tell a linear story.
- **Emotional expression:** Pieces frequently explore feelings, relationships, or social themes in abstract ways.

**Common techniques**

Dancers often train in release technique, Graham and Limón technique, Cunningham technique, contact improvisation, and Gaga (developed by Ohad Naharin). Most also take ballet to build strength and control.

**Where you'll see it**

Contemporary dance appears in professional companies, dance competitions, music videos, theater, and TV shows like *So You Think You Can Dance*, where its lyrical, emotional style became widely popular.

In short, contemporary dance is less about a strict set of steps and more about exploring how the body can move and communicate.

"All work and no play makes Jack a dull boy" is an old English proverb. It first appeared in print in James Howell's *Proverbs* in 1659. The point is simple: a life with nothing but labor wears people down and makes them less interesting, less creative and less happy.

There are several good reasons the saying holds true:

**Rest restores the mind.** Concentration is a limited resource. Working without breaks causes mental fatigue, which hurts focus, memory and decision-making. Downtime lets the brain recover and come back sharper.

**Play fuels creativity.** Many insights arrive when you aren't trying to force them, such as on a walk, during a game or in the shower. Play encourages experimentation and loose thinking, and those are hard to reach under constant pressure.

**Variety makes a person interesting.** Hobbies, friendships, travel and fun give people stories, perspectives and passions beyond their job. Someone who only works has little else to talk about, and that is the "dull" part of the proverb.

**Burnout is real.** Chronic overwork is linked to stress, exhaustion, poor sleep, health problems and, ironically, lower productivity. Play is not wasted time. It is part of what keeps people able to work at all.

**Relationships need time.** Social play builds the connections that support well-being.

It's worth noting that a lesser-known later addition balances the saying: "All play and no work makes Jack a mere toy." The real lesson is balance. Work gives life purpose and structure, and play keeps it rich, healthy and human.

The line is also famous for its chilling use in *The Shining*, where it is typed over and over, which shows just how badly things can go when the balance is lost.

One quick note before the list: Mariya Takeuchi debuted in 1978, so she does belong to the late-70s scene, but most of her best-known songs actually come from the 1980s and later. Her career has lasted more than four decades, and her signature sound sits at the center of what is now called "city pop." The songs below cover her whole career, with the 1970s material marked so you can focus on it if your assignment requires.

## Late 1970s – Early 1980s (RCA years)

**"Modotte Oide, Watashi no Jikan" (1978)**
Her debut single. It's a breezy, polished pop song that introduced her as a college-aged singer with a clear, warm voice. Not her biggest hit, but important as the start of her career.

**"September" (1979)**
One of her signature early songs, written by Takao Kisugi with lyrics by Takashi Matsumoto. It's a bittersweet song about a relationship fading as summer turns to autumn. It earned her wide recognition and remains a fan favorite.

**"Watashi no Heart wa Stop Motion" (1979)**
An upbeat single used in a cosmetics commercial, which helped make her a household name. It shows the bright, idol-adjacent side of her early image.

**"Fushigi na Peach Pie" (1980)**
Probably her biggest hit of the RCA era. Also tied to a cosmetics campaign, it's playful and catchy, with a sunny pop arrangement. If you need one song to represent her earliest fame, this is a strong choice.

**"Sweetest Music" (1980)**
From the album *Miss M*, which was partly recorded in Los Angeles with American session musicians. The song reflects how closely her sound was linked to West Coast AOR at the time.

## Mid-1980s (after her marriage to Tatsuro Yamashita)

In 1982 she married musician and producer Tatsuro Yamashita, took a break from performing, and returned as a songwriter who wrote most of her own material. Yamashita produced and arranged much of her later work.

**"Plastic Love" (1984)**
From the album *Variety*. This is now her most famous song worldwide. It was only a modest success on release, but around 2017 an unofficial upload on YouTube went viral, and the song became the face of the global city pop revival. Its funky bassline, disco-influenced groove and lonely lyrics about a woman who hides her heartbreak in nightlife have been endlessly covered and remixed.

**"Mou Ichido" (1984)**
Another single from *Variety*, a mid-tempo ballad that showed her growing strength as a songwriter.

**"Genki wo Dashite" (1984 / 1987)**
She originally wrote this for actress-singer Hiroko Yakushimaru, then recorded her own version on the album *Request* (1987). It's a gentle, encouraging song telling a friend to cheer up after a breakup, and it's one of her most beloved tracks in Japan.

## Late 1980s – 1990s

**"Single Again" (1989)**
A dramatic ballad about running into a former lover after both of their lives have changed. It was used as a TV drama theme and became one of her biggest commercial hits.

**"Kokuhaku" (1990)**
Another drama-linked ballad, emotionally heavy and very popular, continuing her success with mature love songs.

**"Junai Rhapsody" (1994)**
A major hit that was included on the compilation *Impressions*, which sold several million copies and is one of the best-selling albums in Japanese history.

**"Camouflage" (1998)**
Used as the theme for a TV drama, this song topped the Oricon charts and showed that she was still commercially strong two decades after her debut.

## 2000s and Later

**"Inochi no Uta" (2008 / 2012)**
Originally written for an NHK drama under a pen name, this song about gratitude for life later became widely known in her own recording and is often sung at ceremonies in Japan.

**Recent albums**
*Denim* (2007), *Trad* (2014) and *Precious Days* (2024) show she has kept releasing new material, though she rarely tours.

## Suggestions for Your Assignment

- If the focus is strictly the 1970s, use "Modotte Oide, Watashi no Jikan," "September," and "Watashi no Heart wa Stop Motion," and mention "Fushigi na Peach Pie" as the 1980 peak of that period.
- If the focus is her overall popularity, "Plastic Love," "Single Again," and "Genki wo Dashite" are essential.
- If the focus is cultural impact, "Plastic Love" is the key case study, since its online rediscovery is a good example of how the internet revived interest in older Japanese pop for an international audience.

Because release years and chart details sometimes vary between sources, it's worth double-checking specific dates against an official discography or the Oricon database before citing them.

**Free Speech Lawyer Blasts Ruling Denying The Slants a Trademark**

A federal appeals court's refusal to let an Asian-American band trademark its own name is being sharply criticized by First Amendment attorney Marc Randazza, who says the decision undermines free speech and reflects a culture that has grown too quick to take offense.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit upheld the Patent and Trademark Office's decision to deny registration to The Slants, a Portland, Oregon, dance-rock band founded by Simon Tam. The trademark office had rejected the application under a provision of federal trademark law that bars marks that "may disparage" people, concluding that the name was likely to offend people of Asian descent.

Tam has said the band chose the name deliberately, to take back a slur long aimed at Asian-Americans and turn it into a badge of pride.

Randazza argues that the court got it wrong. Trademarks, he says, are commercial speech, and commercial speech is protected by the First Amendment. The government may police trademarks that are confusing or deceptive, in his view, but it should not withhold protection from a name simply because some people find it insulting.

The outcome carries an obvious irony: a band of Asian-American musicians has been told it cannot register the word it uses to describe itself because that word is offensive to Asian-Americans.

Randazza called the ruling a sign of our easily offended times, in which discomfort is increasingly treated as a reason to restrict expression.

The case echoes the dispute over the Washington Redskins, whose trademark registrations the trademark office canceled in 2014 on similar grounds.

The fight may not be over. In a separate opinion, one member of the three-judge panel suggested the court should reconsider its long-standing precedent holding that refusing a trademark does not raise First Amendment concerns.
